claim: Trophoblast organoids (TOs) and decidua organoids (DOs) were successfully generated from mid-to-late gestation (26-41 weeks of gestation) human placentas.
source: To generate matched human TOs and decidual organoids (DOs), we used human placental tissue isolated from the second and third trimesters of human pregnancy (26–41 weeks gestation) and cultured progenitor cells isolated from chorionic villi or uterine glands of the decidua (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure used to generate organoids from specific gestational age tissue, supported by the methods and results sections.

claim: Organoids were successfully isolated from all 15 unique placentas harvested.
source: Although the abundance of trophoblast stem/progenitor cells decreases after the first trimester (Turco et al., 2018), we successfully isolated progenitor cells and generated organoids from all placental tissue harvested (15 unique placentas).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental success rate with specific numbers provided.

claim: The abundance of trophoblast stem/progenitor cells decreases after the first trimester.
source: Although the abundance of trophoblast stem/progenitor cells decreases after the first trimester (Turco et al., 2018), we successfully isolated progenitor cells and generated organoids from all placental tissue harvested (15 unique placentas).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Turco et al., 2018.

claim: Ki67 positive cells were identified in full-term chorionic villi used to generate TOs.
source: Consistent with the presence of progenitor cells in full-term chorionic villi, we identified cells positive for the proliferation marker Ki67 in villi isolated from two late gestation placental villi used to generate TOs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TOs and DOs were highly proliferative based on Ki67 immunostaining.
source: Once established, organoids could be continuously expanded and passaged every 3–5 days for DOs and 5–7 days for TOs and were highly proliferative based on Ki67 immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TOs expressed the trophoblast-specific marker SIGLEC6 but DOs did not.
source: This also included the expression of the trophoblast-specific marker Sialic Acid Binding Ig Like Lectin 6 (SIGLEC6) in TOs but not DOs and the expression of the mucin MUC5AC in DOs but not TOs (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: DOs expressed the mucin MUC5AC but TOs did not.
source: This also included the expression of the trophoblast-specific marker Sialic Acid Binding Ig Like Lectin 6 (SIGLEC6) in TOs but not DOs and the expression of the mucin MUC5AC in DOs but not TOs (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: TOs expressed high levels of Syndecan-1 (SDC-1), a specific marker of the fused syncytiotrophoblast (STB).
source: TOs also expressed high levels of Syndecan-1 (SDC-1), a specific marker of the fused STB (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The apical surface of the STB in TOs is inward facing.
source: The localization of SDC-1 in TOs shows that like organoids derived from first trimester placental tissue (Turco et al., 2018), the apical surface of the STB is inward facing (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SDC-1 localization data shown in Figure 1—video 1 and comparison to previous work.

claim: TOs, but not DOs, secreted the trophoblast-specific hormone hCG.
source: We also found that TOs, but not DOs, secreted the trophoblast-specific hormone hCG as assessed by Luminex assays and over the counter (OTC) test strips (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data and OTC test strip results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The levels of hCG were stable in TOs propagated for extended periods of time.
source: The levels of hCG were stable in TOs propagated for extended periods of time (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal hCG measurement data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: DOs released high levels of the secreted mucin MUC16, which was not present in TOs.
source: In addition, we confirmed that DOs released high levels of the secreted mucin MUC16 as determined by Luminex assays, which was not present in TOs (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EVT differentiation significantly increased the presence of HLA-G positive cells in TOs from ~18% to ~96%.
source: Similarly, we found that this differentiation process significantly increased the presence of HLA-G positive cells in TOs isolated from full-term tissue (from ~18% positive cells to ~96% positive cells) (Figure 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Elevated levels of matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) were detected in media collected from EVT differentiated TOs.
source: Consistent with an enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs, we detected elevated levels of matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), which is expressed at high levels in first trimester EVTs (Isaka et al., 2003; Shimonovitz et al., 1994), in media collected from EVT differentiated TOs (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 1I and citations to previous work.

claim: MMP-2 is expressed at high levels in first trimester EVTs.
source: Consistent with an enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs, we detected elevated levels of matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), which is expressed at high levels in first trimester EVTs (Isaka et al., 2003; Shimonovitz et al., 1994), in media collected from EVT differentiated TOs (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Isaka et al., 2003 and Shimonovitz et al., 1994.

claim: TOs and DOs were transcriptionally distinct based on differential expression analysis using DESeq2 followed by principal component analysis (PCA).
source: We found that TOs and DOs were transcriptionally distinct based on differential expression analysis using DESeq2 followed by principal component analysis (PCA) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, C.

claim: TOs highly expressed transcripts specifically enriched in the placenta, including HSD3B1, XAGE2 and 3, GATA3, and ERVW-1, which were absent or expressed at very low levels in DOs.
source: TOs highly expressed transcripts specifically enriched in the placenta, including HSD3B1, XAGE2 and 3, GATA3, and ERVW-1, which were absent or expressed at very low levels in DOs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D, E.

claim: TOs highly expressed transcripts for PSGs, ERVW-1, and CGA, which were not expressed in DOs.
source: In addition, TOs highly expressed transcripts for PSGs, ERVW-1, and CGA, which were not expressed in DOs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The levels of expression of placental transcripts in TOs were comparable to those in primary human trophoblasts (PHTs).
source: The levels of expression of these transcripts were comparable to those in primary human trophoblasts (PHTs), confirming that TOs recapitulate the transcriptional signature of primary trophoblasts (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative RNASeq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DOs expressed markers associated with the decidua and decidual stromal cells, including MUC1, MUC5A, MUC5B, SOX17, and HOXB8 which were absent or expressed at low levels in TOs and PHT cells.
source: In contrast, DOs expressed markers associated with the decidua and decidual stromal cells, including MUC1, MUC5A, MUC5B, SOX17, and HOXB8 which were absent or expressed at low levels in TOs and PHT cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: miR-516B-5p, miR-517A-3p, and miR-525-5p were expressed at high levels in TOs, comparable to levels observed in freshly isolated chorionic villi, but were not expressed in DOs.
source: We found that miR-516B-5p, miR-517A-3p, and miR-525-5p were expressed at high levels in TOs, comparable to levels observed in freshly isolated chorionic villi, but were not expressed in DOs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The chromosome 19 microRNA family (C19MC) is specifically expressed in the human placenta.
source: To further confirm that TOs and DOs recapitulated their tissues of origin, we profiled the expression of three members of the chromosome 19 microRNA family (C19MC), which are specifically expressed in the human placenta (Mouillet et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mouillet et al., 2015.

claim: TOs isolated from placentas obtained from male fetuses expressed Y-linked genes, which were absent in female-only derived DOs.
source: Finally, we found that TOs isolated from placentas obtained from male fetuses expressed Y-linked genes, which were absent in female-only derived DOs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: TOs most closely clustered with samples derived from first trimester placental tissue based on hierarchical clustering.
source: Hierarchical clustering showed that TOs most closely clustered with samples derived from first trimester placental tissue (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TOs expressed high levels of pregnancy hormones such as CGA and various CGBs similar to first trimester tissue.
source: In addition, TOs expressed high levels of pregnancy hormones such as CGA and various CGBs similar to first trimester tissue and also expressed factors including kisspeptin-10 (KISS1), which is expressed at higher levels in first trimester tissue compared to full-term tissue (Bilban et al., 2004; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 2C and citation to previous work.

claim: Kisspeptin-10 (KISS1) is expressed at higher levels in first trimester tissue compared to full-term tissue.
source: In addition, TOs expressed high levels of pregnancy hormones such as CGA and various CGBs similar to first trimester tissue and also expressed factors including kisspeptin-10 (KISS1), which is expressed at higher levels in first trimester tissue compared to full-term tissue (Bilban et al., 2004; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Bilban et al., 2004.

claim: TOs secreted only two cytokines (IL-6 and IL-28A/IFN-λ2) and three immune-regulated secreted soluble receptors (sTNF-R1, gp130/sIL-6Rβ, and sTNF-R2) at baseline.
source: We found that TOs secreted only two cytokines (IL-6 and IL-28A/IFN-λ2) and three immune-regulated secreted soluble receptors (sTNF-R1, gp130/sIL-6Rβ, and sTNF-R2) at baseline (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based multianalyte profiling data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DOs released 21 immune factors at baseline.
source: By contrast, DOs released a larger number of immune factors overall, with 21 detected in DO-derived CM at baseline (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based multianalyte profiling data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PCA of Luminex profiles identified factors contributing to the differential nature of the secretome between TOs and DOs, which included the enrichment of factors including CXCL1, CXCL5, and IL-8 in DOs versus IL-6 and IL28A/IFN-λ2 in TOs.
source: PCA of these Luminex profiles identified factors contributing to the differential nature of the secretome between TOs and DOs, which included the enrichment of factors including CXCL1, CXCL5, and IL-8 in DOs versus IL-6 and IL28A/IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of Luminex data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Human chorionic villous explants release numerous cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that impact both maternal and fetal antimicrobial defenses.
source: We have shown previously that human chorionic villous explants release numerous cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that impact both maternal and fetal antimicrobial defenses (Corry et al., 2017; Megli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Corry et al., 2017 and Megli et al., 2021.

claim: PHTs isolated from mid-gestation and full-term placentas secrete immunomodulatory factors.
source: Similarly, we have shown that PHTs isolated from mid-gestation and full-term placentas secrete some of these same immunomodulatory factors (Corry et al., 2017; Megli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Corry et al., 2017 and Megli et al., 2021.

claim: TOs recapitulated the phenotype of constitutive release of type III IFNs and released high levels of IFN-λ2, but not type I IFNs or IFN-λ1.
source: We found that TOs recapitulated this phenotype and released high levels of IFN-λ2, but not type I IFNs or IFN-λ1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DOs did not basally secrete any detectable IFNs.
source: In contrast, DOs did not basally secrete any detectable IFNs (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The levels of released IFN-λ2 from TOs were comparable to those from PHT cells and from matched cultured villous explants.
source: The levels of released IFN-λ2 were comparable to those from PHT cells and from matched cultured villous explants (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The release of IFN-λ2 from TOs was detectable by ~10 days post-plating and reached high levels by >14 days in culture.
source: We monitored the release of IFN-λ2 over the growth period of TOs and found that its release was detectable by ~10 days post-plating and reached high levels by >14 days in culture, which correlated with similar trends for IL-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal Luminex assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CM isolated from TOs, but not DOs, induced interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in cells treated with this CM using a HEK293-based reporter assay.
source: We confirmed that CM isolated from TOs, but not DOs, induced interferon-s (ISGs) in cells treated with this CM using a HEK293-based reporter assay (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells.
source: Consistent with this, CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells (Figure 4E) and in DOs (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TO-derived CM exerts potent antiviral effects on non-placental cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ZIKV infection assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CM isolated from TOs reduced ZIKV infection in DOs.
source: Consistent with this, CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells (Figure 4E) and in DOs (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TO-derived CM exerts potent antiviral effects on non-placental cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ZIKV infection assay data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2.
source: Finally, we found that TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2, suggesting that EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs.
source: Finally, we found that TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2, suggesting that EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EVT-differentiated TOs have reduced IFN-λ2 secretion.

claim: Both TOs and DOs robustly responded to poly I:C treatment, which corresponded with significant transcriptional changes as assessed by RNASeq.
source: We found that both TOs and DOs robustly responded to poly I:C treatment, which corresponded with significant transcriptional changes as assessed by RNASeq (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: TOs upregulated 448 transcripts in response to poly I:C treatment whereas DOs upregulated 121.
source: Comparison of the transcripts induced by poly I:C treatment (as defined by significance of p<0.01 and log2 fold-change of ±2) of TOs and DOs revealed that TOs upregulated 448 transcripts whereas DOs upregulated 121 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only 69 transcripts were shared between TOs and DOs in response to poly I:C treatment, the majority of which (64 of 69) were ISGs.
source: Of these, only 69 were shared between TOs and DOs, the majority of which (64 of 69) were ISGs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram and heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: TOs induced the expression of chemokines including CXCL5 (log2 fold change 5.9), CX3CL1 (log2 fold change 7.1), and CCL22 (log2 fold change 7.6) in response to poly I:C treatment, which were the most induced cytokine or chemokine transcripts in poly I:C-treated TOs.
source: Of the differentially induced transcripts, TOs induced the expression of chemokines including CXCL5 (log2 fold change 5.9), CX3CL1 (log2 fold change 7.1), and CCL22 (log2 fold change 7.6), which were the most induced cytokine or chemokine transcripts in poly I:C-treated TOs (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DOs expressed chemokines at high basal levels, which were not further induced by poly I:C treatment and did not induce any CCL22.
source: In contrast, DOs expressed chemokines at high basal levels, which were not further induced by poly I:C treatment and did not induce any CCL22 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Transcripts most selectively induced in DOs by poly I:C treatment included CD38 and the phospholipase PLA1A.
source: Transcripts most selectively induced in DOs included CD38 and the phospholipase PLA1A (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The topmost induced factors in poly I:C-treated TOs were the chemokines CCL22, CXCL5, CXCL2, and CX3CL1.
source: The topmost induced factors in poly I:C-treated TOs were the chemokines CCL22, CXCL5, CXCL2, and CX3CL1 (Figure 5D, left), which was consistent with their transcriptional upregulation by RNASeq (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PCA of Luminex-based profiling of poly I:C treated TOs and DOs revealed organoid-specific responses to this treatment, which included the specific induction of CCL22 in poly I:C treated TOs.
source: PCA of Luminex-based profiling of poly I:C treated TOs and DOs revealed organoid-specific responses to this treatment, which included the specific induction of CCL22 in poly I:C treated TOs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5E and F.

claim: Type III IFNs IFN-λ1 and IFN-λ2 were induced by both TOs and DOs in response to poly I:C treatment and were the topmost induced factors in DOs.
source: Factors induced by both TOs and DOs included the type III IFNs IFN-λ1 and IFN-λ2 (Figure 5G and H), which were the topmost induced factors in DOs.
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Type I IFNs IFN-α2 and IFNβ were induced to significantly greater levels in TOs than DOs in response to poly I:C treatment.
source: In contrast, the type I IFNs IFN-α2 and IFNβ were induced to significantly greater levels in TOs than DOs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: DOs were highly permissive to HCMV infection as quantified by detectable GFP or mCherry expression of viral gene expression in most organoids.
source: We found that DOs were highly permissive to HCMV infection as quantified by detectable GFP or mCherry expression of viral gene expression in most organoids (Figure 6A, C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A, C and D.

claim: TOs were largely resistant to HCMV infection, with low levels of infection by AD169r and almost undetectable levels by TB40E.
source: In contrast, TOs were largely resistant to HCMV infection, with low levels of infection by AD169r and almost undetectable levels by TB40E, as assessed by fluorescence of tagged viral gene expression (Figure 6B, C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B, C and D.

claim: The HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9 and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs.
source: Consistent with this, analysis of the expression of key HCMV products using bulk RNASeq from infected TOs and DOs showed that the HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9, which is important for HCMV DNA replication (Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020), and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: RNA4.9 is important for HCMV DNA replication.
source: Consistent with this, analysis of the expression of key HCMV products using bulk RNASeq from infected TOs and DOs showed that the HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9, which is important for HCMV DNA replication (Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020), and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020.

claim: There was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection in TOs under EVT differentiation conditions despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs.
source: Despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs under differentiated conditions, we found that there was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection under these conditions (Figure 6F and G), suggesting that EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
source: Despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs under differentiated conditions, we found that there was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection under these conditions (Figure 6F and G), suggesting that EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EVT differentiation did not enhance HCMV infection.

claim: TOs responded to HCMV infection through the differential expression of 282 transcripts (AD169r strain) or 173 transcripts (TB40E strain), of which ~38% were shared between both strains of HCMV.
source: TOs responded to HCMV infection through the differential expression of 282 transcripts (AD169r strain) or 173 transcripts (TB40E strain), of which ~38% were shared between both strains of HCMV (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: DOs responded to HCMV infection with 95 (AD169r strain) or 117 (TB40E strain) transcripts differentially expressed by this infection.
source: By contrast, DOs responded to HCMV infection less robustly, with 95 (AD169r strain) or 117 (TB40E strain) transcripts differentially expressed by this infection (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: Only 3-4% of differentially expressed transcripts were shared between TOs and DOs infected with AD169r or TB40E.
source: Of these differentially expressed transcripts, only 3–4% were shared between TOs and DOs infected with AD169r (Figure 7E) or TB40E (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Only three transcripts were induced by both strains of HCMV in both TOs and DOs and included CCNA1 (Cyclin A1), the ISG OAS2, and EPSTI1 (Epithelial Stromal Interaction 1).
source: Of these shared transcripts, only three were induced by both strains of HCMV in both TOs and DOs and included CCNA1 (Cyclin A1), the ISG OAS2, and EPSTI1 (Epithelial Stromal Interaction 1) (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Transcripts specifically induced by HCMV infection of TOs included H3Y1 (H3.Y Histone 1), KHDC1L (KH Domain Containing 1 Like), several members of the PRAME Family (PRAMEF2, 8, 12, 14, and 20), and TRIM49A and B (Tripartite Motif Containing 43).
source: Transcripts specifically induced by HCMV infection of TOs included H3Y1 (H3.Y Histone 1), KHDC1L (KH Domain Containing 1 Like), several members of the PRAME Family (PRAMEF2, 8, 12, 14, and 20), and TRIM49A and B (Tripartite Motif Containing 43) (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: DO-specific transcripts induced by HCMV infection included several components of the nitric oxide signaling pathway including NOS2 (Nitric Oxide Synthase 2), DUOX2 (Dual Oxidase 2), and DUOXA2 (Dual Oxidase Maturation Factor 2) as well as CXCL10 and CSF3/G-CSF.
source: In contrast, DO-specific transcripts included several components of the nitric oxide signaling pathway including NOS2 (Nitric Oxide Synthase 2), DUOX2 (Dual Oxidase 2), and DUOXA2 (Dual Oxidase Maturation Factor 2) as well as CXCL10 and CSF3/G-CSF (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), IL-8, and IL-11.
source: We found that TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment (Breviario et al., 1992), IL-8, and IL-11 (Figure 8A, C and D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 8A, C and D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pentraxin-3 (PTX3) was first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment.
source: We found that TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment (Breviario et al., 1992), IL-8, and IL-11 (Figure 8A, C and D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Breviario et al., 1992.

claim: DOs responded to HCMV infection by secreting both proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., CXCL10, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, and IL-6) and through the release of the type III IFN IFN-λ2.
source: In contrast, DOs responded to HCMV infection by secreting both proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., CXCL10, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, and IL-6) and through the release of the type III IFN IFN-λ2 (Figure 8B, C and E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 8B, C and E, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: DOs did not induce any other detectable IFNs such as IFN-α2 or IFN-β or IFN-λ1 in response to HCMV infection.
source: In contrast to IFN-λ2, DOs did not induce any other detectable IFNs such as IFN-α2 or IFN-β or IFN- λ1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Treatment of DOs with ruxolitinib significantly increased levels of HCMV replication.
source: We found that treatment of DOs with ruxolitinib significantly increased levels of HCMV replication, which correlated with higher levels of GFP fluorescence (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: Treatment of TOs with ruxolitinib did not increase levels of HCMV replication over DMSO treated controls.
source: In contrast, treatment of TOs with ruxolitinib did not increase levels of HCMV replication over DMSO treated controls, which remained low under both ruxolitinib-treated and DMSO-treated conditions (Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Co-culturing of DOs and TOs led to a significant reduction in HCMV infection in DOs compared to singly cultured DOs.
source: We found that whereas singly cultured DOs were permissive to HCMV infection, co-culturing of DOs and TOs led to a significant reduction in HCMV infection in DOs (Figure 8I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8I and J.

claim: PHT cells from full-term placentas and mid-gestation chorionic villi constitutively release type III IFNs, which protect trophoblasts from viral infections.
source: We showed previously that PHT cells isolated from full-term placentas and mid-gestation chorionic villi constitutively release type III IFNs, which protect trophoblasts from viral infections (Bayer et al., 2016; Corry et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Bayer et al., 2016 and Corry et al., 2017.

claim: The decidua may be a primary site of replication for several microorganisms associated with congenital disease, including HCMV, ZIKV, and Listeria monocytogenes.
source: The decidua may be a primary site of replication for several microorganisms associated with congenital disease, including HCMV (McDonagh et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2003; Weisblum et al., 2015), ZIKV (Guzeloglu-Kayisli et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2018; Weisblum et al., 2017), and Listeria monocytogenes (Rizzuto et al., 2017), suggesting it may serve as a reservoir for these infections.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Human trophoblasts constitutively release antiviral interferons (IFNs) that restrict infection in both autocrine and paracrine manners.
source: For example, human trophoblasts constitutively release antiviral interferons (IFNs) that restrict infection in both autocrine and paracrine manners (Bayer et al., 2016; Corry et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Bayer et al., 2016 and Corry et al., 2017.

claim: Constitutive release of IFNs is a unique feature of trophoblasts as IFNs are tightly regulated in most cell types and induced only after detection of the products of viral replication.
source: Constitutive release of IFNs is a unique feature of trophoblasts as IFNs are tightly regulated in most cell types and induced only after detection of the products of viral replication (reviewed in Lazear et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Lazear et al., 2019.

claim: The risk of transplacental transmission of HCMV infection from mother to fetus is only 20% in the first trimester but can reach up to 75% in the third trimester.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Pass and Anderson, 2014.

claim: CXCL10 was highly upregulated in HCMV-infected DOs, consistent with prior findings of increased CXCL10 secretion in decidua explants infected with HCMV ex vivo.

claim: Type III IFNs control HCMV infection in the maternal decidua.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the ruxolitinib treatment experiments showing that inhibiting IFN signaling increases HCMV infection in DOs.

claim: Additional factors or pathways beyond IFN signaling may restrict HCMV infection of trophoblasts.

claim: Ablation of type III IFN signaling in the murine placenta enhances infection of ZIKV in maternal decidua tissue.
source: Indeed, ablation of type III IFN signaling in the murine placenta enhances infection of ZIKV in maternal decidua tissue (Jagger et al., 2017).

claim: Trophoblast-derived effectors, including IFN-λ, work in paracrine to suppress HCMV infection in cells comprising the maternal decidua.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-culture experiments showing that TOs protect DOs from HCMV infection.

claim: Human trophoblasts and mid-gestation chorionic villi respond to T. gondii infection through the selective release of CCL22.
source: We have shown previously that human PHTs and mid-gestation chorionic villi also respond to T. gondii infection through the selective release of CCL22 (Ander et al., 2018; Rudzki et al., 2021), suggesting that this chemokine may be key mediator of the response of the human placenta to microbial infections.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Ander et al., 2018 and Rudzki et al., 2021.

claim: CCL22 induction may directly impact maternal-fetal tolerance in the context of congenital infection.
source: Given that Treg infiltration into the decidua has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including miscarriage (Freier et al., 2015), CCL22 induction may directly impact maternal-fetal tolerance in the context of congenital infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CCL22 is a Treg chemoattractant and Treg infiltration is associated with adverse outcomes.

claim: Treg infiltration into the decidua has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including miscarriage.

claim: HCMV is a species-specific β-herpesvirus that can only infect humans.
source: HCMV is a species-specific β-herpesvirus that can only infect humans, and animal models using guinea pig (GPCMV) or rhesus macaque (RhCMV) cytomegaloviruses rely on viruses that are genetically disparate from HCMV and do not fully recapitulate the human maternal-fetal interface (Roark et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and a citation to Roark et al., 2020.

claim: Animal models using guinea pig (GPCMV) or rhesus macaque (RhCMV) cytomegaloviruses rely on viruses that are genetically disparate from HCMV and do not fully recapitulate the human maternal-fetal interface.

claim: Isolation and propagation of trophoblast stem cells from first trimester placental chorionic villi lead to the development of three-dimensional organoids that differentiate to contain all lineages of trophoblast cells present in the human placenta and release well-known pregnancy hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).

claim: Infections at the maternal-fetal interface can directly harm the fetus and induce complications that adversely impact pregnancy outcomes.

claim: The placenta forms a powerful barrier to infections.
